methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective cohort study with 119 de novo FL patients and 16 transformed FL patients. Clear inclusion/exclusion criteria, FFPE sample collection at diagnosis from two centers, NGS-based TMB assessment using validated 409-gene panel. Statistical analysis includes Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis tests, Cox proportional hazards models with assumption testing, and model performance evaluation (C-index, CPE, BIC, AIC). Optimal cutoff determination using maxstat package. Limitations acknowledged: targeted panel vs. WES, variable commercial availability, AID-associated mutations in Ig regions not captured.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual retrospective cohort study (LoE 2b) with direct clinical relevance to FL prognostication. Identifies TMB as independent prognostic biomarker for PFS, LSS, OS in non-ICT setting (standard immunochemotherapy). Addresses unmet clinical need: ~20-30% of FL patients have poor prognosis POD24 not well-identified by current indices (FLIPI, FLIPI-2). Plausible translational path via treatment selection (potential ICI combinations mentioned). However, causality not established; observational biomarker association only.

reporting_quality.justification: Well-reported observational cohort study following STROBE principles. Patient demographics (Table 1), clinical endpoints clearly defined (PFS, LSS, OS per Lugano criteria). Methods detail NGS workflow: 409-gene panel specifications, variant calling filters (VAF≥5%, depth≥60), germline removal using multiple databases. Results include mutation landscape overview, statistical comparisons across groups, survival curves (Kaplan-Meier implied). Ethical approval documented. Data availability score limited: no mention of data repository, code availability, or plan to share genomic data.

novelty_literature.justification: Study applies TMB concept (recognized in ICI response prediction, emerging as prognostic biomarker in solid tumors) to lymphomas, specifically FL. TMB as prognostic factor in hematologic malignancies is largely unexplored per authors. However, one prior FL study (Tsukamoto et al.) examined somatic mutation counts with conflicting results. Novel aspect: demonstration that high TMB associates with improved PFS/OS in FL independent of FLIPI, and association with migration genes (GNA13/GNAI2) and t(14;18). Incremental contribution to FL prognostication literature.

writing_presentation.justification: Clear, well-organized manuscript with logical flow from introduction (unmet need for FL prognostication) through methods, results, and discussion. Figures effectively present TMB distributions and survival curves. Supplemental figures provide comprehensive mutational landscape data. Discussion contextualizes findings within literature, acknowledges methodological differences vs. prior work, proposes future ICI strategies. Tables 1-2 clearly summarize patient characteristics and outcomes. Minor: some density in genetic pathway descriptions could be streamlined.

key_strengths: Addresses significant unmet clinical need: prognostic biomarker to identify FL patients at high risk of POD24 (20-30% relapse rate not well predicted by existing indices)

Robust statistical analysis: TMB remains independent prognostic factor for PFS, LSS, OS in multivariate Cox models including FLIPI; consistent improvement in model performance metrics (C-index, CPE, BIC, AIC)
Clear risk stratification: low-TMB group (14.3%) shows 33.6% 5-year PFS vs. 71.0% in high-TMB group (p=0.008), with 47.1% POD24 rate in low-TMB vs. 16.3% in high-TMB
Biologically plausible mechanism: TMB as surrogate for neoantigen load driving T-cell immunity; associations with t(14;18), BCL2, TNFRSF14, GNA13/GNAI2 mutations support model
Longitudinal follow-up of 25 paired diagnosis-relapse samples examining TMB stability and clonal dynamics; all POD24 patients with relapse samples showed clonal relationship at baseline
key_concerns: Targeted panel (409 genes, 1.2 Mb coding) vs. whole-exome sequencing gold standard; panel not specifically validated in lymphomas (validated only in solid tumors). Individual variants discretely contribute ~0.8 mut/Mb, raising sensitivity to calling differences near cutoff
Transformed FL cohort (n=16) underpowered for definitive survival analyses; optimal TMB cutoff not determined in this group, limiting prognostic conclusions

Missing methodological details: no prespecified analysis plan, no sample size justification, no adjustment for multiple comparisons in pathway analyses, limited statistical power for rare mutation associations (e.g., TP53 n=3)
Data availability limited: no mention of data sharing plan, genomic data repository, or code availability despite complex bioinformatic workflows

Conflicting literature precedent: Tsukamoto et al. study in FL showed opposite direction (high mutations = worse outcome); no clear resolution of discrepancy beyond methodological differences (AID mutations in Ig regions)
chief_reviewer.rationale: Solid retrospective cohort study addressing genuine clinical unmet need in FL prognostication with rigorous statistical methods and plausible biologic mechanism. LoE 2b appropriate for observational biomarker study. Tier 3 (competent, incremental work) due to retrospective design, targeted panel validation gap, and incremental nature vs. novel methodology. Minor revisions recommended for data-sharing transparency and cutoff sensitivity analysis.
